conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had this sharp pain in my lower left side for about four days now. It’s constant and goes into my back. It’s worse than my usual pancreatitis pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And does the pain get better or worse with eating or moving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, it doesn’t seem to change with food or bowel movements. I’ve also been nauseous and threw up a few times. I haven’t been able to keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any fever, chills, or weight loss?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt like I had a fever, but I didn’t check. I did lose about 20 pounds recently, but I’m not sure why.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. We’ve reviewed your CT scan from today. It shows stable chronic pancreatitis—no new inflammation or blockages. Your liver has some fat, but nothing urgent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not acute pancreatitis? I was worried it might be worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, your lipase is normal, and the CT doesn’t show signs of acute inflammation. This looks like a flare of your chronic condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve had these flares before. But this one’s really painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—for now to let your pancreas rest. You’ll get fluids through your IV and pain meds to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I be NPO?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll reassess tomorrow. Once your pain improves and nausea is controlled, we’ll start with clear liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my diabetes? I usually take pills, but I haven’t eaten.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. We’ve started you on a sliding scale insulin to manage your blood sugar while you’re not eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. And my pain meds—I usually need something strong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started a Dilaudid PCA pump so you can control your pain safely. We’ll monitor it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a celiac plexus block a while back. Did that help? I don’t remember much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you had one recently. It can help, but since your pain is flaring again, we’re focusing on medication and rest for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s your pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but the IV meds are helping. I haven’t vomited since yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Your labs are improving. We’re going to try advancing your diet to clear liquids today if you’re up for it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but I’m nervous. Last time I ate too soon, I threw up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go slow—start with ice chips and broth. If you tolerate it, we’ll build up. We’re also continuing your pancreatic enzymes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pancreaze, right? I take that with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll restart that when you’re on solid food. Also, your EGD showed Grade C esophagitis—reflux is likely contributing to your nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had heartburn for years. I’m on omeprazole and Zantac.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep the omeprazole twice daily, but we’re stopping Zantac. It’s not needed with the higher omeprazole dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, fine by me. Any other changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We consulted the chronic pain team. Given your history, they don’t recommend more procedures. They suggest discussing Suboxone for pain with your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Suboxone? For pain? I thought that was for addiction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can help with chronic pain too, especially in patients with a history like yours. It’s safer than long-term opioids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Huh. I’ll ask my doctor about it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve been on a soft diet since yesterday and no vomiting. Pain is much better, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it’s way better. I’m actually hungry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re going to switch you to oral pain meds—Dilaudid tablets as needed. We’ll watch how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I get a prescription when I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a one-week supply. But no refills. We want you to follow up with your PCP to discuss long-term pain management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. What about constipation? The pain meds always mess me up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adding Miralax and senna—take them as needed to stay regular.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my trazodone—I take 300 mg at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re reducing that to 100 mg as needed. Higher doses can cause side effects, especially with your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try it. I just need to sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. You’ve been tolerating a full diet, and your abdomen is much less tender. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your regular meds except Zantac. Take Dilaudid only as needed for pain, and use Miralax and senna if you’re constipated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your PCP within a week. They’ll review your pain plan and the IgG test we ordered to check for autoimmune pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I have an appointment next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. You look much better—pain is mild, you’re eating well, and your labs improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I feel a lot better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: take the Dilaudid only as needed, stay on your enzymes with meals, and follow up with your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll ask about that Suboxone option.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good idea. Also, call if the pain worsens or you can’t keep food down. Otherwise, take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.
